title: Garbage Disposal Leaking Water — Causes & Fixes
question: Why is my garbage disposal leaking water under the sink, and how do I find where it's coming from and fix it?
summary: A leaking garbage disposal is almost always a loose or worn seal at one of three spots: the top sink flange (where the unit mounts to the sink drain), the side connections (the dishwasher drain hose or the discharge pipe to the P-trap), or — the bad one — the bottom body of the unit itself. The trick is to find the exact spot with a fill-and-dye test before you touch anything. Top-flange and side-connection leaks are cheap, safe DIY reseals. Water dripping from the bottom of the unit or its reset button means an internal seal has failed or the housing is cracked, and the disposal must be replaced, not repaired. Note this is a leak, not a jam — a disposal that hums but won't spin is a completely different fix.

commonCauses.cause: Loose or dried-out sink flange seal at the TOP of the unit. This is the ring where the disposal clamps up to the sink drain opening, sealed with plumber's putty or a rubber gasket. Over years the putty dries and shrinks, or the mounting bolts work loose, and water seeps out the top when the basin holds water. Most common source of a disposal leak.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Dry everything, then plug the sink and fill the basin. Look up at the top of the disposal where it meets the sink drain. Water appearing there while the sink is FULL (before you pull the plug) points to the flange.

commonCauses.cause: Loose or worn discharge-pipe connection on the SIDE. The discharge tube runs from the disposal to the P-trap, held either by a bolted flange with a rubber gasket or a slip-joint nut. A gasket that has hardened or bolts that backed off will drip here, but only while water is actually draining through.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Fill and then drain the sink while watching the discharge outlet on the side of the unit and the P-trap joints. A leak that appears only while the water is RUNNING OUT is the discharge/drain side, not the flange.

commonCauses.cause: Loose dishwasher drain hose connection on the SIDE. If you have a dishwasher, its drain hose clamps onto an inlet on the disposal body. A loose hose clamp, a cracked hose, or (on a brand-new install) a knockout plug that was never removed can leak here, usually most when the dishwasher drains.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the smaller inlet near the top-side of the disposal where a ribbed rubber hose is clamped on. Run the dishwasher (or pour water down it) and watch that clamp and hose for drips.

commonCauses.cause: Cracked disposal body or failed internal shaft seal at the BOTTOM. Age, corrosion, or a hard freeze cracks the housing, or the internal seal above the motor wears out, and water weeps from the very bottom of the unit or around the red reset button. This is not repairable — the unit must be replaced.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Dry the whole unit, run water, then feel the bottom center and the reset button with a paper towel. Water coming from the BOTTOM of the housing (not a connection) means replace it.

commonCauses.cause: Leak is actually the P-trap or drain slip-nuts downstream, not the disposal. A loose slip nut or a shot washer on the trap can drip onto the disposal and run down it, making a healthy disposal look like the culprit. Worth ruling out before you buy a new unit.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Trace the wet path upward with a dry paper towel. If the highest wet point is a trap or tailpiece slip-nut joint downstream of the disposal — and the disposal body above it is dry — the trap is the leak.

fixes: Cut power first: unplug the disposal, or if it's hardwired, switch off its breaker and confirm the switch does nothing. Never reach under the sink with power live, and never put your hand or fingers down into the disposal.

Pinpoint the source with a fill-and-dye test. Dry every surface with paper towels, put a bucket or dry newspaper under the unit, add a few drops of food coloring to a basin of water, then watch: a leak while the sink is FULL = top flange; a leak only while DRAINING = a side/discharge connection; water at the BOTTOM of the unit = internal/cracked (replace).

Tighten the obvious connections. For a discharge or drain leak, snug the discharge-flange bolts evenly, or hand-tighten slip-joint nuts plus about a quarter turn with pliers. Many leaks are just a connection that loosened over time. Re-test before doing more.

Fix the dishwasher hose: tighten or replace the hose clamp, and swap a cracked or stiff drain hose (a few dollars). On a new install where the dishwasher never drained, make sure the knockout plug inside the disposal inlet was actually removed.

Replace the discharge-pipe gasket if tightening didn't stop it. Undo the discharge flange, drop in a fresh rubber gasket ($3-$8), and re-bolt evenly. Replace worn trap/tailpiece washers at the same time if the drain side was leaking.

Re-seat the top sink flange if that's the source. Support and drop the unit off its mounting ring, scrape off the old plumber's putty, apply a fresh rope of plumber's putty under the flange (or the correct fiber/rubber gasket some brands use — check your model), reset the unit, and tighten the mounting bolts evenly all the way around. Wipe the squeeze-out.

If the leak is from the BOTTOM of the housing or the reset button, stop — the internal seal is gone or the body is cracked and it cannot be resealed. Replace the whole unit (match the horsepower; 1/3-3/4 HP is typical). A plug-in model is the easiest DIY swap; hardwired means disconnecting the electrical, which is where less-confident folks should call a plumber.
After ANY fix, run the dye test again and watch for a full minute of filling and draining before you call it done. Then check the cabinet floor over the next day or two — dry means fixed.
Don't let a leak sit. Standing water rots the cabinet base and can reach the outlet or the unit's wiring, turning a cheap seal job into water and electrical damage.
diyVsPro: Mostly DIY. Running the dye test, tightening connections, replacing a dishwasher hose or a discharge gasket, and re-seating the sink flange with fresh plumber's putty are all safe and low-skill with the power off — no soldering, no gas, no high voltage. Even swapping the entire unit is a common weekend DIY job, easiest on plug-in models where you just unplug, unbolt, and reverse. Call a plumber if: the disposal is hardwired and you're not comfortable disconnecting the electrical, the leak is from the bottom of the unit and you'd rather not lift it out yourself, the leak has been soaking the cabinet or reached the outlet, or you find rot, mold, or persistent leaks after resealing.
typicalCostUSD: DIY parts: plumber's putty $3-$6, discharge/flange gasket $3-$8, hose clamp ~$2, dishwasher drain hose $8-$15. A replacement disposal unit runs $80-$250 for a standard 1/3-3/4 HP model ($250-$400 for premium quiet models). Pro: a plumber service call is roughly $90-$200; a reseal or reconnect is about $100-$250; a full disposal replacement installed typically runs $150-$450 including the unit.
timeEstimate: Diagnosis with the dye test 15-30 min. Tightening a connection or swapping a hose/gasket 30-60 min. Re-seating the sink flange about 1 hour. A full unit replacement is 1-2 hours DIY, or a single plumber visit.
safetyNote: A garbage disposal is a 120V electric motor sitting right next to water, so treat the power seriously: unplug it, or if it's hardwired switch off its breaker AND confirm the wall switch is dead before you reach underneath — and if you're disconnecting hardwired leads, verify they're de-energized with a voltage tester. NEVER put your hand or fingers into the disposal, powered or not; the impellers can injure you. Water pooled in the cabinet near the outlet or the unit's wiring is a shock hazard — cut power and dry it up before working. This is not a gas appliance and there is no 240V or roof work involved, so it stays firmly in DIY territory, but if you're uneasy about the electrical disconnect or the leak is from the bottom of the unit (meaning replacement), a licensed plumber is a reasonable call.
toolsParts: Bucket or dry newspaper and plenty of paper towels/rags
Food coloring (to trace the leak in the dye test)
Screwdrivers (flat and Phillips) for the hose clamp and flange bolts
Hex/Allen wrench or the disposal's mounting wrench
Plumber's putty (and/or the correct flange gasket for your model)
Replacement discharge-pipe gasket and trap/tailpiece washers
Replacement dishwasher drain hose and hose clamp (if needed)
Non-contact voltage tester (to confirm power off on hardwired units)
Replacement disposal unit, 1/3-3/4 HP, if the body is cracked
